item.title: The/Nudge secures $15M from Google.org to develop AI tools for small businesses
item.description: Google.org is committing $15 million to The/Nudge to develop AI tools that help Indian small businesses access credit, markets and compliance support, alongside local skills training.
item.content:encoded:
The/Nudge, an Indian action institute focused on livelihoods and economic inclusion, is receiving a $15 million funding commitment from Google.org, Google’s philanthropic arm, to develop artificial intelligence (AI) tools for India’s micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs).

The funding aims to improve access to formal credit, market opportunities, and regulatory compliance for small businesses.

The programme will include an open call for proposals to identify practical solutions to business challenges. It will also develop a multilingual, voice-led platform to train people in Tier III and IV towns in job-ready skills and connect them with small businesses.

Google’s announcement estimates that more than 90 million small businesses in India employ over 345 million people, although many continue to face difficulties securing finance and reaching digital markets.

Preeti Lobana, Google India’s Vice President and Country Manager, said the AI technology must address everyday business needs. “For AI to be truly successful in India, it must become a practical multiplier for the millions of small businesses that drive our economic growth,” she said.

The funding comes amid growing investment in technology-led lending to small businesses. In February, Chennai-based Prayaan Capital raised Rs 110 crore in a Series A round led by venture capital firm Peak XV Partners to build a technology-enabled lending platform. In October 2025, Bengaluru-based Optimo Capital raised Rs 150 crore from founder Prashant Pitti and existing investors Blume Ventures and Omnivore, alongside separate debt funding of Rs 110 crore from IDFC and Axis Bank.

Subhashree Dutta, Chief Executive of the^delta, an organisation supporting social entrepreneurs, said the initiative would use “stage-gated grand challenges”, meaning competitive rounds with defined milestones, to support solutions across compliance, market access, quality and credit. She argued that these barriers reinforce one another.

Dutta also said the initiative’s open standards could make MSMEs more competitive, creditworthy and globally visible.

Government initiatives are also targeting the sector’s financing and technology constraints. The IndiaAI Mission, approved in 2024 with an outlay of Rs 10,371.92 crore over five years, supports computing capacity, skills, startup financing, and AI applications. In October, the Union Cabinet approved a separate Rs 10,000 crore SME Growth Fund for direct equity investment in growth-oriented businesses.

Public-sector banks are also using digital credit assessments based on verifiable business data. Official figures show that 98,995 MSME loan applications were sanctioned under this model between April 1 and July 15, 2025.

item.title: TechSparks 2026 Day 2: From Krishna Byre Gowda’s Bengaluru blueprint to Stripe’s global playbook, and more
item.description: TechSparks 2026 Day 2: Krishna Byre Gowda on tech-led governance and metro plans, Stripe on going global, VCs on deeptech bets.
item.content:encoded:
On the second day, the 17th edition of TechSparks 2026 in Bengaluru moved between policy and product, with conversations on governance, the city’s infrastructure future, global-first startups, and India’s deeptech opportunity.

YourStory’s flagship startup-tech summit brought together founders, investors, policymakers, and technologists to explore how India can build for itself and for the world.

The day’s headline conversation featured Krishna Byre Gowda, Minister for Greater Bengaluru Development, Government of Karnataka, in a fireside chat with Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO, YourStory and The Bharat Project. Drawing on his time in the state’s Land Revenue Department, Gowda said technology in governance can minimise corruption and help bridge the trust gap between citizens and the government.

“The more technology we adopt in governance, the better will be our delivery of services to people, and lower will be the levels of corruption,” he said.

He also cautioned that technology alone cannot fix systemic problems without a shift in civic behaviour. Out of an estimated 35 lakh to 50 lakh properties in Bengaluru, he noted, only 23 lakh have registered khatas and just 18 lakh pay property taxes.

The minister also laid out an ambitious plan for the city’s growth. The state government aims to expand Bengaluru’s metro network from 96 km to 170 km over the next 18 months, and hopes to reach 400 km by 2037, the year the city turns 500. Planning is already underway for a 2,000 sq km area around Bengaluru, well beyond the 750 sq km covered by the Greater Bengaluru Authority.

“Hopefully, in the next six months, we can show demonstrable results in making Bengaluru relatively a cleaner city,” Gowda said.

Moving to global ambitions, Manish Maheshwari, Managing Director, Stripe India, said AI is making it faster and cheaper to build world-facing companies from India, giving rise to what he called the “minimum viable company.” According to him, Indian founders can now go global from day one.

He pointed to Emergent hitting $100 million in ARR in eight months, and Stripe data showing 76% of customers prefer paying in their own currency. Maheshwari also confirmed Stripe’s agreement to acquire OpenRouter, which routes AI queries to the most suitable model, a bet on helping companies control fast-rising AI costs.

“In some of the new-age companies, the amount of money people are spending on tokens is more than what they are spending on salaries,” he said.

Deeptech took centre stage in a panel featuring Vishesh Rajaram of Speciale Invest, Mayuresh Raut of Seafund, Anirudh Singh of Avatar Venture Partners, and Abhishek Srivastava of Kae Capital. The investors said deeptech is giving rise to new kinds of founders, driven by India’s talent advantage and the geopolitical push for self-reliance in critical technologies.

Raut said there is still an eight-to-10-year window of opportunity, while Rajaram noted that “nerve and patience” set apart the founders who endure.

Day 3 of TechSparks 2026 will continue to unpack how India can build, own, and scale the technologies of the new tech order. The agenda features conversations on rethinking engineering education with Prof Ashok Jhunjhunwala, building global companies from day one with Omio’s Naren Shaam, AI sovereignty and the next 500 million users, climate innovation in energy, water, and clean air, and India’s $100 billion AI opportunity, before the summit closes with a fireside chat with Zakir Khan.

item.title: How can students succeed in an AI world? Intel, Sri Chaitanya leaders weigh in
item.description: At TechSparks 2026, leaders from Intel and Sri Chaitanya outlined how replacing rote learning with AI mentorship, emotional resilience, and equitable hardware access can prepare India’s 247 million students for tomorrow.
item.content:encoded:
Educating 247 million primary and secondary students presents a monumental challenge, but as Sushma Boppana, Chief Executive Officer of Sri Chaitanya Group of Institutions, and Santhosh Viswanathan, Vice President and Managing Director for APJ at Intel, pointed out, India’s most urgent hurdle is structural rather than purely numerical.

While traditional Indian schooling remains largely anchored in nineteenth-century methods, society has rapidly jumped from the information age straight into the intelligence era.

A central flaw of legacy education is treating computer skills as an isolated laboratory subject. In contrast, modern enterprise requires a seamless blending of technical tools and daily tasks.

“When you come into the real world... you don't have... work time and... tech time. Tech and work are merged together and I think that's the biggest shift that we all have to start to make,” Viswanathan explained, speaking at a fireside chat with Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO, YourStory and The Bharat Project at TechSparks 2026, YourStory’s annual summit.

Instead of viewing digital tools as an auxiliary feature, learning systems must embed technology natively into everyday instruction, the Intel leader noted.

Although online educational material is now abundant, maintaining student interest remains the primary bottleneck. Artificial intelligence (AI) presents a solution through hyper-personalised learning, which is essentially tailoring instruction to an individual's unique passions, pacing, and native language.

“If someone likes cricket and they want to learn quantum mechanics through cricket, you should have the option... that is very much possible with the AI that is there,” Viswanathan noted.

Crucially, digital mentors like Sri Chaitanya’s AINA deliver friendly, non-judgemental feedback, guiding children without causing demotivation or offence.

Also Read
India can build any technology, says Prof. Ashok Jhunjhunwala; calls for backing startup risk-takers

Systemic reform

As automated tools handle routine tasks, academic test scores are losing their status as the sole benchmark of future success. Student aspirations are evolving from securing traditional jobs toward developing creative problem-solving capabilities and entrepreneurial drive.

Drawing on Sri Chaitanya’s reach of two million offline and online learners, Boppana emphasised that character traits now outweigh pure test performance.

“In this generation if we are able to build up resilience, engagement, accountability these are the three aspects which are more important than academic education,” Boppana noted.

Cultivating resilience requires parents and educators to treat setbacks as essential learning opportunities rather than fearing failure.

“We are more afraid of them failing than them failing... all the failures are what makes a child resilient, not the successes or not the wins,” Boppana observed.

Furthermore, parents must avoid projecting their unfulfilled professional ambitions onto their children. 

Adapting to young learners also requires updating teaching methods to suit modern digital habits.

“If it’s a 30-second Instagram Reel mindset to learn, then our learning and tools need to adapt to the 30-second Instagram Reel mindset to teach,” Viswanathan noted.

Simultaneously, teacher training must focus on empathetic guidance. Modern educators are taught to highlight student strengths before identifying areas for growth.

Meanwhile, systemic progress requires bridging critical infrastructure gaps across the country. India currently suffers from a severe compute deficit.

Viswanathan highlighted this, asking, “Why is compute penetration less than 10% in India? Versus 95% in the US, 75% in China... There is this gap about rich compute creation usage that we need to start to inculcate.”

Addressing this hardware shortage is vital to prevent early loss of learning, particularly among ambitious rural students.

With a large number of young Indians entering the workforce over the coming years, reforming the national educational framework is both an urgent social duty and an extraordinary opportunity.

Viswanathan highlighted this national imperative, saying, “There are 250 million kids in this country that are going to come in in the next 5 years... saying, ‘What is my livelihood going to be?’... It is not only the most profitable problem to solve, but it is also the most significant problem for us to solve.”

By combining empathetic human mentorship with accessible AI infrastructure, India can transform its massive youth population into a global engine of creative innovation.

item.title: Stripe India MD on why Indian startups should build for the world from day one
item.description: At TechSparks 2026, Manish Maheshwari, Managing Director of Stripe India, says AI is making it faster and cheaper to build a world-facing company from India, and that Stripe's OpenRouter deal is aimed at the cost side of the ledger.
item.content:encoded:
Ask Manish Maheshwari what has changed for Indian startups with global ambitions, and his answer is speed. Speaking at the 17th edition of TechSparks, the Managing Director of Stripe India said AI is changing how quickly, and how cheaply, a company can start selling to the world.

"We are seeing the creation of a new way of operating, the minimum viable company," Maheshwari told Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO of YourStory and The Bharat Project, in a fireside chat on taking startups from early traction to global scale. "The entrepreneurs in India can think global and go global on day one now." The financial infrastructure platform helps companies of all sizes manage their payments.

Maheshwari had examples ready. Emergent, he said, reached $100 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR) in eight months, and Pocket FM has recently crossed half a billion in ARR. "If you had asked me two years ago which companies were hitting that level of revenue that fast, I could not have told you," he said.

Stripe's own numbers point the same way. Over the past five years, Maheshwari said, the number of companies using Stripe Atlas, its incorporation and compliance service, to collect money from more than 100 countries has quadrupled. And for most businesses, over a quarter of revenue now comes from outside their top 10 markets.

Stripe, valued at $160 billion and still pre-IPO, pitches itself as the layer that takes the pain out of all this. Maheshwari said founders should not be burning engineering hours on payments plumbing. "As a founder, you want to focus on your core product," he said. "If you are spending your engineering time customising your financial infrastructure, maybe you are not using your engineering in the best way." Stripe's idea, he said, is to make money programmable "through a single API". Founders need not even travel. "You can sit in India and sell to the world, and earn foreign exchange for your country."

Localisation, he argued, is where the money is. Stripe's data shows 76% of customers prefer to pay in their own currency, and that offering local payment methods beyond cards lifts revenue by roughly 12%. "You are leaving 12% of the money on the table by not offering them," he said. It matters for physical goods too, he added, pointing to Purely Copper, which makes copper bottles in India, has built a following in the US, and takes payments through Stripe before shipping.

The OpenRouter bet

Maheshwari confirmed that Stripe has agreed to acquire OpenRouter, a platform that routes AI queries to the most suitable model. The logic, he said, is that AI bills are climbing fast. "In some of the new-age companies, the amount of money people are spending on tokens is more than what they are spending on salaries."

Stripe already helps companies earn money through subscriptions, usage-based billing and invoicing. OpenRouter would help them keep a lid on what they spend. "If you want to build a solid P&L, you need great revenues, but you also have to keep your costs in control," he said. "That is when you make a profit."

Agents and checkout

An audience member asked whether AI agents will finally be able to complete payments on their own. Maheshwari said agentic commerce is "becoming more and more mainstream", at least in the US. He said Stripe's one-click payment product, Link, lets users authorise an agent to spend within a set limit, and that Stripe is helping shape payment protocols for agent-led shopping. "Stripe has a ringside view of this because we are integrated into all the major AI companies," he said. Retailers, he added, are already redesigning their websites so they are "machine readable as well" as human friendly.

item.title: ‘We cannot wait 75 years’: ANRF CEO Shivkumar Kalyanaraman on scaling India’s research multiplier
item.description: To boost India’s R&D spend toward 3% of GDP, ANRF CEO Shivkumar Kalyanaraman revealed a patient-capital architecture combining private investment, open IP licensing, and national mission programmes.
item.content:encoded:
India cannot afford to replicate the 75-year evolutionary timelines of Western institutions like the US National Science Foundation or DARPA, according to Shivkumar Kalyanaraman, Chief Executive Officer of the Anusandhan National Research Foundation.

Speaking at TechSparks 2026, YourStory’s annual summit, Kalyanaraman made it clear that under an impatient Prime Minister, the organisation must bypass traditional bureaucratic friction and drive scientific discovery into the real economy at unprecedented speed.

Describing the foundation as an institutional startup, Kalyanaraman outlined how the nation is altering its approach to scientific research and technology commercialisation. Formalised by parliament in 2023 following recommendations in the National Education Policy 2020, the foundation operates as an autonomous statutory body presided over by the Prime Minister of India.

The organisation was established to transform the country into a global innovation powerhouse by linking higher education, private industry, venture capital, and global philanthropy, ensuring rapid funding flows from foundational research to market implementation.

Patient capital

At the centre of this financial transformation is the Research, Development, and Innovation fund, a government-backed pool of Rs 1 lakh crore. Designed as a patient capital instrument, the fund provides long-term financial support tailored to research-intensive and deep-tech enterprises that require extended gestation periods without demanding immediate short-term returns.

Instead of disbursing capital directly to individual businesses, the foundation acts as an apex funding architecture that routes money through secondary fund managers.

Under this fund-of-funds structure, an initial allocation is provided to nineteen selected fund managers and specialised statutory entities, which in turn attract additional private investment. This arrangement creates a financial multiplier expanding capital reaching real-world technology ventures.

“This is a patient capital fund and our Rs 1 lakh crore of government money or taxpayer money will catalyse a lot more anywhere from Rs 5 to 10 lakh crores by the time it hits the real economy,” he said.

To complement government allocations, the foundation aggregates corporate social responsibility grants, diaspora contributions, and global philanthropic partnerships.

The ultimate objective is to raise national expenditure on research and development from sub 1% of gross domestic product to 3% or more through a compound annual growth rate of 20 to 25%.

Democratising excellence

Beyond commercial capital, the foundation addresses structural imbalances across the higher education sector. Historically, advanced scientific research in India remained concentrated within a small cluster of elite institutions, such as the Indian Institutes of Technology and the Indian Institute of Science.

Pointing to the need for broader participation, Kalyanaraman noted, “India has a very tiny sliver of institutions that are deep in R&D and deep in the excellence of R&D. So, we would like to broaden this distribution, but our goal is not just to throw money at different places, but to really broaden the distribution of excellence.”

To achieve wider distribution without lowering standards, the foundation launched the Partnerships for Accelerated Innovation and Research initiative. This framework uses a hub-and-spoke mentorship structure in which top-tier research universities guide regional institutions from Kashmir to Nagaland.

To ensure academic research yields practical benefits, the foundation established targeted sectoral initiatives known as Maha programmes covering electric mobility, medical devices, space technology, artificial intelligence for science, drones, water security, and critical minerals.

A major bottleneck in commercialisation has been transferring intellectual property from universities to commercial startups. To resolve this, discoveries under programmes like artificial intelligence for science are released under open licensing frameworks derived from the MIT licence model, allowing startups to rapidly adopt university research and de-risk laboratory discoveries at regional translational test facilities.

item.title: Peak XV is taking bigger bets as Indian startups grow more ambitious: Mohit Bhatnagar
item.description: At TechSparks 2026, Peak XV's Managing Director Mohit Bhatnagar said the venture capital firm is increasingly willing to back ambitious, high-risk startups as AI opens up new opportunities for Indian founders to build global companies.
item.content:encoded:
Indian startup founders are increasingly aspiring to build companies worth $50 billion or even $100 billion, a shift that is prompting venture capital firms such as Peak XV Partners to take bigger risks, according to its Managing Director Mohit Bhatnagar.

During a fireside chat with Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO of YourStory and The Bharat Project, at TechSparks 2026 in Bengaluru, Bhatnagar said the success of companies such as Zomato and the growing acceptance of startups in India's public markets have fundamentally changed what founders and investors believe is possible.

Bhatnagar was gungo-ho about the ambition and aspiration of Indian founders which has grown multifold over the years. "The startup ecosystem is in a much better place today than it was 20 years back. The biggest difference is in ambition," he said.

According to him, the ambition of startup founders is at a different level now than what was seen in the past. Bhatnagar, who has two decades of experience as a venture capitalist, sees ambition from Indian startups only getting bigger going forward.

Peak XV is one of the leading venture capital firms in the country with investment bets spread across sectors, including companies such as Zomato and Meesho.

Bhatnagar said Peak XV has had about 37 IPOs in the country, and 22 of them have happened in the last five years.

“The total market cap of all startups that have gone public in India today is somewhere around $170 billion. That number, by the way, used to be 1/10 or much smaller than that 10 years back,” Bhatnagar remarked and added that public markets are embracing startups like never before.

“The Indian public markets in the last five years have truly been a massive blessing to the entire startup ecosystem,” he remarked.

There have also been other changes across the world, driven by artificial intelligence (AI).

Bhatnagar believes AI can be a big advantage for a country like India. “AI tools are now available to everybody. Everyone here should be dreaming about building a company that is rooted in India and really think global,” he said.

He emphasised that every founder should leverage the AI opportunity to build global companies. He highlighted that, as the cost of tokens fall over a period of time, consumer AI applications will be unleashed across sectors such as health, financial services, and education.

He was also of the firm opinion that AI will bring in efficiency as smaller teams will be able to quickly come out with better solutions.

At the same time, he said, there is no easy yardstick to identify the right companies. Founders need to sustain their hard work to build a durable business, which might take even a decade.

Bhatnagar said India remains a very attractive destination for investors seeking to back startup founders. “I really hope we now see a 10x unleashing of entrepreneurial energy because it's become so much easier to launch a product, to try it in the marketplace, than ever before. You don't need as much capital.”
